production.title: Tesla's Flying Roadster Is Really a Balloon Trick

narration:
Tesla says its new Roadster can fly,
and this week it showed something closer to a jump.
That jump works like a balloon you blow up and let go,
which shoots off because the air rushing out the back pushes it forward.
So the Roadster carries ten small jets
fed by six hundred litres of compressed air.
Then at the reveal in Texas, that push lifted it up a ramp,
spun it, and carried it over a row of Tesla cars.
The physics behind it is Newton's third law,
which says every push comes with an equal push back.
Inside, the air is squeezed into carbon-fibre tanks at very high pressure,
and when a valve opens it blasts out of the jets,
shoving the car the opposite way, just like the balloon.
Point the jets at the ground and the car rises.
But a balloon empties in seconds,
and a heavy car burns through its air just as fast,
so you get a hop, not a trip across town.
Before you believe the word flying, ask how long the air lasts.
If that helped, follow us,
because we break down one tech story every day.
And the next time a balloon zips across your room, you'll know how Tesla's Roadster flies.

research.summary: Tesla revealed the second-generation Roadster on 15 October 2026 near Waco, Texas. Ten cold-gas thrusters fed by 600 litres of compressed air lifted it up an inverted ramp, spun it and hopped it over other Tesla vehicles. Production is promised for 2028; reservations cost $50,000 (Performance) and $250,000 (Thrust). Physics analysts say cold-gas thrust lasts seconds, so it is a hop, not sustained flight; no FAA approval has been reported. Musk said safety 'is not the main goal'.

metadata.title: How Tesla’s Flying Roadster Actually Works
metadata.description:
Tesla’s new Roadster used compressed-air thrusters to jump, spin and fly over a row of Tesla cars. But how does a heavy electric car lift off like a balloon?

This short explainer breaks down the ten air jets, carbon-fibre tanks and Newton’s third law behind Tesla’s flying car demo—and why it is more of a short hop than a practical flight.
